ratings.reviewer_notes: Directly shows that the microbial SCFAs butyrate and acetate protect in vitro intestinal barrier function from LPS-induced disruption and alter tight-junction abundance and morphology.
Butyrate supplementation directly improved intestinal barrier integrity and tight-junction protein abundance in broiler chickens while altering caecal SCFA concentrations.

Acetate-, propionate-, and butyrate-producing strains increased SCFAs and enhanced intestinal tight-junction protein expression in DSS colitis, although strain effects are not separable from their metabolites.
Dimethyl itaconate concurrently improved gut barrier markers and increased propionate, butyrate, and their producing bacteria, providing indirect rather than metabolite-specific evidence.
Direct ex vivo human study of microbial-derived butyrate and colonic permeability; it found no acute protection against induced hyperpermeability and reduced claudin-1 expression at 25 mM.
Focused review describing microbial butyrate as a regulator of gastrointestinal tight-junction proteins and a potential barrier-restoring metabolite in IBD.
Direct sodium butyrate supplementation increased intestinal occludin and morphological barrier integrity and reduced permeability-related serum LPS in alcohol-fed mice.
Directly identifies butyrate as protective for tight junctions and mucosal barrier function through suppression of oxidative stress/Notch signaling, with dose-dependent effects.
Direct cecal propionate infusion enhanced jejunal morphology and increased claudin-1, claudin-4, and occludin, linking propionate to intestinal barrier function.
Direct cell-model evidence that butyrate protects against LPS-induced barrier impairment and increases claudin-3 and claudin-4 through Akt/mTOR-associated mechanisms.
Directly compared butyrate, acetate, propionate, and succinate; only butyrate alleviated cytokine-induced barrier dysfunction, principally by limiting claudin-2 upregulation.
Review-level synthesis specifically covering gut microbial metabolites as regulators of the intestinal barrier in IBD, but the abstract does not identify individual metabolites.
Discusses acetate, butyrate, and propionate in relation to blood-brain barrier integrity rather than intestinal barrier integrity.
Probiotic-induced increases in acetate, butyrate, and propionate correlated with restoration of intestinal tight-junction proteins in food-allergic mice, though metabolite causality was not isolated.
Direct mechanistic evidence that butyrate enhances intestinal barrier function by SP1-dependent claudin-1 transcription and redistribution of ZO-1 and occludin.
Review-level sepsis context identifies butyrate as a colonocyte fuel and intestinal barrier stabilizer and discusses SCFA trafficking through tight-junction-regulated pathways.
Porcine-focused review links acetate, propionate, and butyrate to tight-junction expression, mucus production, intestinal morphology, and barrier integrity.
Review summarizes mechanisms through which microbiota-derived short-chain fatty acids act on multiple intestinal barrier components.
Rifaximin increased microbiome-derived butyrate, and direct in vitro experiments showed butyrate increased epithelial MUC2, supporting intestinal barrier strengthening.

Probiotic treatment increased acetic and butyric acids alongside tight-junction restoration through an AMPK/MLCK-associated axis in aging mice, although direct metabolite intervention was not performed.

Increased butyrate was associated with enhanced intestinal and blood-brain barrier integrity after decoction treatment, but direct butyrate experiments focused on microglial inflammation rather than the intestinal barrier.
Polysaccharide treatment improved the intestinal barrier and increased acetate, propionate, butyrate, and isobutyrate, but the metabolite-barrier relationship was not directly tested.
Review-level evidence identifies acetic acid, propionic acid, and butyric acid as microbial metabolites influencing intestinal tight-junction proteins.
